To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) an "immediate shutdown" power management strategy outperforms sophisticated adaptive strategies; (ii) service times of requests affect the effectiveness of power strategies; (iii) an upper bound exists on the additional latency caused by power management strategies, and; (iv) the upper bound is tight.

(1) the latency of an embedded system is a function of the service time of arriving requests and the power management strategy, (2) the performance of a power management strategy depends on the service time distribution of the system, (3) an "immediate shutdown" strategy performs better than adaptive algorithms for a wide range of service time distributions, and (4) the additional latency of a system introduced by a power management algorithm is bounded by the length of the longest idle period in the system.

the "immediate" power management strategy outperforms sophisticated algorithms in the presence of bursty traffic, and that power management strategies increase system latency by an amount proportional to the number of times the system is shut down.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and analyzing power management algorithms for embedded systems.
the design and analysis of online power management strategies for embedded systems.
the design of algorithms for power management and their analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
power management is a very complex problem.
the performance of a system is dependent on the service time and arrival rate distribution of the system.
the performance of a system depends heavily on the characteristics of the arrival process, service times and the power management algorithm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more aggressive the system shutdown policy the greater is the increase in latency of the system and the less effective the power management strategy.
power management is a very complex problem that has to be analyzed in the light of the system's requirements and characteristics.
the performance of a power management algorithm is a complex interaction of system parameters and the algorithm's behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a power management algorithm can be effective without knowledge of future requests and without knowledge of service time distributions.
the performance of power management algorithms can vary greatly depending upon the service times of the requests, the latency of the requests, and whether the algorithms are adaptive or not.
a power management strategy should be chosen based on the service times of the system, and not on the number of components in the system.
